Abstract: 38

39

Background: 40

Households are a major setting for SARS-CoV-2 infections, but there remains a lack of 41

knowledge regarding the dynamics of viral transmission, particularly in the setting of widespread 42

pre-existing SARS-CoV-2 immunity and evolving variants. 43

44

Methods: 45

We conducted a prospective, case-ascertained household transmission study in the greater 46

Boston area in March-July 2022. Anterior nasal swabs, along with clinical and demographic 47

data, were collected for 14 days. Nasal swabs were tested for SARS-CoV-2 by PCR. Whole 48

genome sequencing was performed on high-titer samples. 49

50

Results: 51

We enrolled 33 households in a primary analysis set, with a median age of participants of 25 52

years old (range 2-66); 98% of whom had received at least 2 doses of a COVID-19 vaccine. 53

58% of households had a secondary case during follow up and the secondary attack rate (SAR) 54

for contacts infected was 39%. We further examined a strict analysis set of 21 households that 55

had only 1 PCR+ case at baseline, finding an SAR of 22.5%. Genomic epidemiology further 56

determined that there were multiple sources of infection for household contacts, including the 57

index case and outside introductions. When limiting estimates to only highly probable 58

transmissions given epidemiologic and genomic data, the SAR was 18.4%. 59

Conclusions: 61

Household contacts of a person newly diagnosed with COVID-19 are at high risk for SARS- 62

CoV-2 infection in the following 2 weeks. This is, however, not only due to infection from the 63

household index case, but also because the presence of an infected household member implies 64

increased SARS-CoV-2 community transmission. Further studies to understand and mitigate 65

household transmission are needed. 66

INTRODUCTION 69

70

In March 2022,  the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant BA.2 and its descendants caused multiple 71

outbreaks across the greater Boston area of Massachusetts1. More than 95% of the population of 72

Massachusetts at that time had received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, and a large 73

number of individuals had been infected with the Omicron BA.1 variant only a few months 74

prior1. Despite this presence of partial population immunity, there were over 200,000 new 75

COVID-19 cases reported in Massachusetts between March and July 2022, coincident with the 76

dropping of mask requirements and a reduction in social distancing policies. 77

78

Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, households have been a major setting for SARS-CoV-2 79

transmission2. A meta-analysis of 135 studies published in 2022 found that the secondary attack 80

rate (SAR) – the risk of transmission from index case to household contact – of exposed 81

household contacts was 30-36% during the Alpha and Delta SARS-CoV-2 waves and 43% 82

during the early (BA.1) Omicron period2. Factors associated with transmission risk were the 83

vaccine status of the exposed contact, household density (i.e., the number of people sleeping in 84

the same room), and immunological factors such as the magnitude of cross-reactive memory T 85

cells to SARS-CoV-2 antigens3-5. In general, the SARs reported in households, and other 86

residential settings6, have been far higher than reported in other settings such as schools, where a 87

SAR of 2.8% was reported for exposed students in 10 Massachusetts schools during the Delta 88

wave7. 89

Despite the large number and range of household studies performed to date, there remains a lack 91

of precision and detail regarding the dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 household transmission.  These 92

studies are each individually small in size, and most lack careful characterization on the genomic 93

level. This uncertainty is particularly important in the increasingly common scenario where there 94

is (1) widespread pre-existing SARS-CoV-2 immunity, either from vaccination or infection, (2) 95

emergence of new SARS-CoV-2 strains that are partially immune evasive, and (3) few infection 96

control precautions in home and community environments. Knowing the risk of household 97

transmission in this scenario, as well as identifying factors that can predict lower SARs, would 98

enhance our ability to counsel patients appropriately and meaningfully reduce SARS-CoV-2 99

infections in households. 100

101

To address this research gap, we conducted a household SARS-CoV-2 transmission study in the 102

greater Boston area in March-July 2022 in which we used clinical, demographic, viral kinetic, 103

and genomic data for high-resolution analyses of SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics. 104

105

METHODS: 106

107

We conducted a prospective, observational, case-ascertained transmission study of household 108

contacts of index SARS-CoV-2 cases identified in the greater Boston and Chelsea areas of 109

Massachusetts in the United States. The primary recruitment pathway was via ambulatory 110

COVID-19 testing sites associated with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC). 111

Ethics 114

The BIDMC Committee on Clinical Investigation, its Institutional Review Board (IRB), 115

approved the study protocol (#2022P000021). Consent procedures were completed via 116

phone/video conferencing or in-person. All enrolled participants provided verbal informed 117

consent. Participants who met applicable IRB guidelines for provision of assent underwent an 118

age-appropriate assent process; informed consent for study participation was obtained from each 119

participant’s parent or legal guardian before any study-specific procedures were performed. 120

Sequencing of SARS-CoV-2-positive specimens was covered under protocol #1612793224, 121

reviewed and approved by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) IRB. 122

123

Study Population 124

An index case was eligible for inclusion if the participant (1) had a positive SARS-CoV-2 test 125

either by rapid diagnostic assay or RT-PCR no more than 5 days prior to enrollment and had no 126

more than 5 days of acute respiratory illness symptoms prior to testing, and (2) lived, and had 127

plans to live in his/her household for the follow-up period of 14 days, and (3) was not 128

hospitalized and had not been hospitalized since the date of illness onset, and (4) was at least 2 129

years old. An index case was excluded from the study if the participant did not live in a 130

household (e.g., lived alone or in a congregate setting), or if they reported that any other person 131

in the household had an acute respiratory illness or tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 in the 7 days 132

before the test date or illness onset date of the index case. 133

134

A household contact was eligible for inclusion if the participant (1) routinely slept (at least half 135

of the nights in the last month) in the same household as the index case, and (2) slept in the 136

Respiratory Specimen Collection 141

Each enrolled index case and household member self-collected an anterior nasal swab 142

(Rhinostics dry swab in a sterile tube; https://rhinostics.com/) on each day of the 14-day follow- 143

up period. The swab was self-collected regardless of whether the individual had acute respiratory 144

illness signs or symptoms. Samples were dropped off by the participants at the BIDMC Clinical 145

Research Center or the Chelsea clinic. A subset of participants who were treated with 146

nirmatrelvir-ritonavir were asked to extend the follow-up period and continue self-swabbing for 147

an additional 7 days in order to monitor for potential virologic rebound8. 148

Questionnaires 150

At enrollment, each consenting household member and index case, or his/her parent/guardian, 151

was asked to provide information on participant demographics, recent exposures to COVID-19, 152

presence of high-risk conditions, prior and current symptoms of COVID-19, COVID-19 153

vaccination status, household characteristics, interactions with other enrolled and non-enrolled 154

household members and people outside the home, and other social or medical history, including 155

other vaccination history, as deemed appropriate. An optional follow-up questionnaire was 156

administered to participants on days 7 and 14. 157

SARS-CoV-2 Viral Load Quantification 160

Viral loads were measured with the Quaeris SARS-CoV-2 Assay, a real-time reverse 161

transcription polymerase chain reaction (rRT–PCR) test, using the Luna Probe One-Step RT- 162

qPCR Kit (No ROX) [NEB E3007]9. The SARS-CoV-2 primer and probe set detects RNA from 163

the SARS-CoV-2 N1 and RdRP genes, and uses the human RNase P gene as a positive control. 164

When received by the laboratory, samples were rehydrated with 300 µl phosphate buffered saline 165

(PBS), inactivated at 65ºC, and subsequently used directly as input for the Quaeris assay without 166

extraction. rRT-PCR was performed on an Applied Biosystem QuantStudio 7 instrument 167

(software version 1.7). Liquid handling was automated using either the Tecan Fluent 1080, the 168

Hamilton Star, or the Multidrop combi dispenser. N1 gene cycle threshold (Ct) values are 169

reported. Viral rebound was defined as at least 2 negative (Ct≥35) PCR results followed by at least 170

2 positive (Ct<35) results. 171

172

SARS-CoV-2 Whole Genome Sequencing 173

Anterior nasal swabs that were positive for SARS-CoV-2 with Ct values of maximally 32 via the 174

Quaris assay were sequenced as previously described10. Briefly, following inactivation with 175

Buffer AVL, RNA was extracted from the samples using the MagMAX mirVana Total RNA 176

Isolation Kit for the Kingfisher Flex (Thermo Fisher #A27828) according to the manufacturer’s 177

instructions. The ARTIC v4.1 primer set was used to amplify SARS-CoV-2 genetic material, 178

from which Illumina DNA Prep sequencing libraries were prepared and sequenced on the 179

NextSeq 55011. 180

SARS-CoV-2 Genomic Data Analysis 183

Sequencing reads were demultiplexed, filtered to remove adapter and contaminant sequences, 184

depleted of reads mapping to the human genome, and assembled by alignment to the reference 185

sequence NC045512.2 via the viral-ngs v2.1.33 pipeline12. The following optional inputs were 186

used with the assemble_refbased workflow to accommodate amplicon-based sequencing: 187

major_cutoff = 0.5, min_coverage = 20, skip_mark_dupes = TRUE, and trim_coords_bed = 188

“gs://pathogen-public-dbs/v1/amplicon_primers-ARTICv4.1_NC_045512.2.bed". 189

190

Lineages were assigned to viral genomes using Pango v4.1.3 pango-data v1.1713. Consensus 191

single nucleotide variants (SNVs) were determined after removing ambiguous sites and sites 192

prone to amplicon sequencing error14. Intrahost single nucleotide variants (iSNVs) were called 193

using LoFreq and were filtered as follows: (i) masking of known problematic sites in SARS- 194

CoV-2 genome, (ii) site read depth of minimally 100; (iii) allele frequency of minimally 3%; and 195

(iv) no evidence of strand bias (via Fisher’s exact test with p > 0.05)11,15. 196

197

Transmission Analysis 198

To infer the relatedness of cases within a household, the most complete genome (i.e., the genome 199

with the highest percentage of unambiguous sites) was used for each person with a minimum 200

unambiguous genome length of 15,000 bp. The genetic (SNV) distance between pairs of cases was 201

used alongside the serial interval, viral kinetics, iSNV information, and test status of other 202

individuals at baseline to classify households into transmission categories. All pairs of cases within 203

each household were assessed, excluding those inconsistent with the longitudinal testing data. 204

Transmissions were categorized as highly probable, possible, or unlikely. Pairs with a genetic 206

distance of less than 2 SNVs and an iSNV in a putative donor that reached consensus in the putative 207

recipient (i.e., transmission of a minor variant through a tight transmission bottleneck) were 208

considered highly probable16,17. An index-contact pair in the strict analysis set (i.e., from a 209

household with a single infected participant and documented PCR- contacts at baseline) with a 210

genetic distance of less than 3 SNVs and a serial interval of less than 7 days were also considered 211

highly probable transmissions. Pairs with a genetic distance of less than 3 SNVs and a serial 212

interval of less than 7 days, but without iSNV support, were categorized as a possible transmission, 213

though we cannot rule out a non-household recent common ancestor (i.e.., a shared exposure)18,19. 214

Pairs with a genetic distance of 3 or more SNVs or a serial interval of minimally 7 days were 215

considered unlikely. Highly probable and possible transmission links were plotted.20,21 216

Phylogenetic Analysis 218

Contextual genomes (10 BA.1 sequences each from Massachusetts and the United States, and 50 219

BA.2 sequences each from Massachusetts and the United States, isolated between 2022-02-01 and 220

2022-08-01) were downloaded from NCBI GenBank. These sequences, along with the most 221

complete genome assembled per study participant (of minimally 15,000 bp), were aligned to the 222

reference sequence (NC_045512.2) using Nextclade v.2.14.122. A phylogenetic tree was estimated 223

using IQ-TREE v.2.2.2.623 and was visualized and annotated using ggtree v.3.8.224 in R v.4.3.1. 224

RESULTS 227

228

Screening, Enrollment, and Follow-up 229

Enrollment began on March 3, 2022 and continued until July 9, 2022, after local SARS-CoV-2 230

case counts had declined1. We enrolled 38 households containing 38 index cases and 77 231

household contacts; Figure 1. One household was subsequently found to be ineligible and 4 232

households did not complete 14 days of follow up. The remaining 33 households (33 index cases 233

and 66 household contacts) constituted our primary analysis set; 85% of these households 234

(28/33) had all household members participate. Of the 33 households in the primary analysis set, 235

3 households had an index case that was PCR- at the time of first research swab, and 9 236

households had at least one household contact that were PCR+ at the time of first research swab. 237

The remaining 21 households (21 index cases and 40 PCR- household contacts) constituted our 238

strict analysis set. The median number of persons per household in the primary analysis set was 239

3.5 (range, 2-5; Supplementary Table 2). The median house size was 1400 square feet (range, 240

740-3300; Supplementary Table 2). 241

SARS-CoV-2 Sequencing 273

For the primary analysis set, approximately 1300 total anterior nasal swab samples were 274

collected and analyzed via the rRT-PCR Quaris assay. 181 of these samples, from 48 unique 275

individuals across 26 unique households, had a diagnostic Ct under 32 (mean = 30.1) and were 276

thus subject to genomic sequencing. 178/181 (98.3%) samples had a nonzero unambiguous 277

assembly length with a median length of 29,321bp. 143 samples, which came from 44 unique 278

individuals among 24 unique households, produced partial genomes of at least 15,000 bp in 279

length (Supplemental Table 4). 15 households yielded partial genomes from multiple individuals 280

within the household. The vast majority of the sequences were BA.2 descendants, consistent with 281

national trends (Figure 2B), though a BA.1 sequence was collected early in enrollment. 282

Focusing first on analyzable households in the strict analysis set (N=6), we found that four 284

households had viral sequences that were either identical between index and secondary cases or 285

differed by only 1-2 SNVs (Figure 3A, Supplemental Table 5). In these cases, transmission from 286

index to secondary case was considered highly probable. In two households, we identified 287

infected with BA.2.12.1; there was a 13 SNV difference between sequences. In household 291

WMD, the index case was infected with BA.2.12.1, and the contact was infected with BA.2; 292

there was a 20 SNV difference between sequences. (Of the 3 remaining households with 293

secondary cases in the strict analysis set (AXB, JDU and NKF), sequences were not available or 294

couldn’t be analyzed; viral kinetic curves for these households are in Figure 3C). When 295

DISCUSSION 326

327

Here we studied the transmission dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 within households using 328

prospective daily PCR surveillance, clinical and demographic data, and genomic epidemiology. 329

Our study is well-positioned to reflect the transmission dynamics of households consisting of 330

relatively young, healthy individuals with pre-existing immunity to SARS-CoV-2. It was 331

conducted during a wave of Omicron BA.2 and its sub-lineages. Our study population consisted 332

primarily of families with 2-5 members; 23% of our participants were children in elementary or 333

middle school. Participants were highly vaccinated, having received a median of 3 COVID-19 334

vaccines. Only 10% had a known prior COVID-19 diagnosis and the population was overall very 335

healthy. 336

337

Our study found that the risk of SARS-CoV-2 in exposed households is very high, consistent 338

with previous reports. In our primary analysis set, we found that 58% of enrolled households 339

went on to have a second SARS-CoV-2 case in the household over the next 2 weeks. Nearly a 340

third of households had a positive secondary case identified on the very first day of testing. At 341

In this analysis, we identified 9 cases among 40 household contacts, or a SAR of 22.5%. Using 350

genomic epidemiology, we then excluded 2 cases as these were likely acquired outside of the 351

household. We thus determined that SAR was 18.4%. Our study was conducted when multiple 352

BA.2 descendants were circulating, and this genetic diversity improved our ability to rule out 353

putative transmission events. 354

355

Using genomic epidemiology across all the households, we found that the infectious source of 356

secondary cases was varied. The most common source of infection was the index case, but other 357

sources included an imported case (outside the household), shared exposures with the index, or 358

other infected contacts within the home. Our findings, particularly evidence of shared exposures 359

and imported cases, highlight that infection within a household serves as a proxy for broader risk 360

for community transmission, emphasizing the importance of maintaining vigilant public health 361

measures both inside and outside of the home. More public health attention should be focused on 362

mitigating this risk via vaccination and therapeutic advances, enhanced and early case detection 363

and isolation, and non-pharmaceutical interventions such as masking and ventilation. 364

SAR estimates have varied considerably across multiple studies, due to varying study designs, 366

populations, and circulating SARS-CoV-2 variants. During the Alpha and Delta waves, the SAR 367

for exposed household contacts was reported between 30-36%, rising to 43% during the early 368

(BA.1) Omicron period2. Here we report that during a BA.2 wave (and its descendants), the SAR 369

was 39% using a larger primary set of households, 22.5% with a strict set of households, and 370

18.4% when further incorporating genomic data. This lower estimate using genomic data is 371

likely a more accurate reflection of the true risk of household exposure. 372

373

Our small sample size substantially limited our power to assess predictors of transmission, 374

especially because prior COVID-19 vaccination was near universal in our study cohort. Given 375

the complexity of estimating the magnitude of pre-existing SARS-CoV-2 immunity by history 376

alone, particularly in the context of both infection and prior vaccines, future household 377

transmission studies would benefit from larger cohorts and baseline immunologic assessments of 378

humoral, cellular and mucosal immune responses. 379

380

In summary, we determined that the risk of household transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is very 381

high, even when using genomic epidemiology to exclude imported cases. Further interventions to 382

block household transmission should be studied, especially in the now-common scenario when 383

population immunity and vaccine coverage are high but viral variants are increasingly immune 384

evasive. 385
